Title: Trump Hands Victories to Putin, Who Offers More War in Return

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/europe/russia-putin-trump-diesel-ukraine.html

Published Time: 2026-10-13T15:03:17.000Z

Markdown Content:

[SKIP ADVERTISEMENT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/europe/russia-putin-trump-diesel-ukraine.html#after-top)

News Analysis

Russia has reaped a diesel deal and an increase in U.S. pressure on Ukraine as President Trump’s political needs align with his longstanding inclinations toward Russia.

Listen

· 8:52 min

![Image 1: Vladimir V. Putin, wearing a dark suit and seated in a white armchair in front of a blue backdrop, leans on his left arm and speaks into a microphone while gesturing with his right hand.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/multimedia/13int-russia-putin-01-htqf/13int-russia-putin-01-htqf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in Moscow this month.Credit...Igor Ivanko/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Published Oct. 13, 2026 Updated Oct. 14, 2026, 1:03 a.m. ET

The wins for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia came in rapid succession from Washington.

President Trump proffered sanctions relief for Russian diesel fuel. He publicly called for Ukraine to get a new leader. And he pressured Kyiv to stop a strike campaign against Russian oil facilities that has damaged the Russian economy.

Mr. Putin, in return, offered more war.

Minutes after Mr. Trump announced the diesel deal, the Kremlin reiterated Mr. Putin’s stance that he would not negotiate with Ukraine at the moment, because he remained angry about Ukrainian strikes during last month’s Russian parliamentary election.

The next day, Russia launched an attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 22 people, including four children. It was the latest in a near [daily drumbeat of devastating Russian strikes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world/europe/russia-ukraine-war-attack-bus.html), which have dramatically increased the civilian toll in Ukraine as Kyiv sorely lacks air-defense missiles.

And Mr. Putin has signaled that he plans to escalate further, [aiming to knock out Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/world/europe/russia-ukraine-winter.html) in what Ukrainians expect to be the worst winter of the war.

Mr. Putin is reaping his victories as Mr. Trump’s own domestic political needs align with his longstanding inclination to tip the scales toward Russia. With the American president focused on trying to bring down fuel prices before a difficult midterm election, he is pushing Kyiv to trade away its leverage for nothing in return.

Image

![Image 2: Emergency workers using powerful flashlights walk across a mound of rubble and through the wreckage of a destroyed building.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/multimedia/13int-russia-putin-02-htqf/13int-russia-putin-02-htqf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Rescue workers at the site of an airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.Credit...Reuters

Ukraine has said it would suspend its oil refinery strikes if Russia ceased attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities heading into the winter. But when Mr. Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” on Sunday, he meant only a suspension of oil refinery strikes in both countries, [The New York Times reported](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/europe/russia-ukraine-war-us-diesel-deal-negotiations.html). Ukraine has only one major oil refinery, and Russian strikes took it largely out of service in 2022.

Mr. Trump has promoted his energy deal with Mr. Putin as an example of how he is tackling America’s diesel challenge, which experts say is more attributable to the war with Iran. But it was seen as a betrayal by Ukrainian officials, undercutting years of Western efforts to starve the Russian war machine of cash.

It may not even do much to lower diesel prices. Economists have said the amount of fuel discussed is not enough to move the needle significantly.

“The U.S. president is focused on one thing, which is himself and his reading of the world,” said Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.

**Want to stay updated on what’s happening in Russia and Ukraine?** , and we’ll send our latest coverage to your inbox.

That reading, Mr. Gabuev said, includes Mr. Trump’s stubborn denial that his own decision to go to war against Iran caused fuel prices to skyrocket. “In his picture of the world, the Gulf war doesn’t play a role in the current diesel crisis, and there needs to be a magical solution with someone he is predisposed to, who is Vladimir Putin.”

Image

![Image 3: President Trump walking on an airport tarmac with Air Force One on the right. A handful of people, some in military uniform, and a presidential limousine, are beyond him.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/multimedia/13int-russia-putin-03-htqf/13int-russia-putin-03-htqf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

President Trump in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday. In recent days, he offered sanctions relief for Russian diesel fuel, called for a new Ukrainian president, and pressured Kyiv to stop hitting Russian oil facilities.Credit...Kenny Holston/The New York Times

Earlier this year, things were looking difficult for Mr. Putin. Expenditures on the war were rapidly expanding. Progress on the battlefield had slowed to a crawl. Global prices for oil, Russia’s top export, had slumped to around $60 a barrel.

Then Mr. Trump launched the war in Iran, alongside Israel. Oil prices jumped to over $100 a barrel. The vast use of air defense missiles by the United States and its Gulf allies in response to Iran’s attacks dried up the supply for Ukraine, leaving it increasingly vulnerable. With Mr. Trump looking for a way out, Russia’s longstanding relationship with Iran offered Mr. Putin a new calling card with Washington.

As the Iran war accorded benefits to Russia, Ukraine tried to limit Moscow’s economic gains with increasingly effective strikes on oil refineries — the campaign that Mr. Trump is now demanding that Kyiv end.

Kyiv’s systematic targeting of Russian oil infrastructure brought the war home to Russia as never before, causing lines at the pump across the country and forcing Russia, one of the world’s largest diesel suppliers, to suspend exports.

As Ukrainian strikes decreased production, Russia’s tax revenue from oil and gas for the first three quarters of the year fell by 17 percent compared with the same period in 2025, even as fuel prices rose dramatically. (A rise in the ruble and Russian domestic fuel subsidies also played a role.)

Now, the diesel deal could pour billions of dollars into the Russian economy. An extended suspension of Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, if Kyiv agrees to one under the intense American pressure, could generate much more money.

Image

![Image 4: Dense, dark smoke billows from a burning industrial site.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/multimedia/13int-russia-putin-04-htqf/13int-russia-putin-04-htqf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Smoke rising from a burning oil refinery in Moscow in June. Strikes on Russian oil facilities over the last few months have disrupted the Russian economy.Credit...via Reuters

The wins for Mr. Putin go beyond the diesel deal. Mr. Trump has also welcomed Russian ministers this year for Group of 20 events in North Carolina and Wisconsin, and he plans to host Mr. Putin in December at the G-20 summit in Miami. His administration is also [negotiating potential business deals with the Kremlin](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world/europe/trump-russia-oil-deal-lukoil-middle-east-investors.html), in what Mr. Trump’s team has cast as inducements to a peace deal.

The Russians want even more from the U.S. president, analysts say.

When Mr. Trump returned to office in 2025, Moscow hoped that the United States would cut off all support for Ukraine and force President Volodymyr Zelensky into a capitulation largely on the Kremlin’s terms.

Mr. Trump’s Oval Office blowup with Mr. Zelensky in March of last year made it seem as if Moscow’s dream was within reach. The Trump administration’s decision to halt weapons donations to Ukraine and suspend intelligence sharing stoked hopes even further.

But in the months since, U.S. intelligence sharing resumed. Mr. Trump brokered a deal for the Europeans to buy weapons from the United States for Ukraine. And U.S.-led peace negotiations fizzled as the Trump administration became distracted by the war in Iran.

Fyodor Lukyanov, a Russian political scientist who advises the Kremlin, wrote last month that Ukraine would be left with little defense if the United States completely ceased its military support.

“But Trump is unlikely to take that step,” Mr. Lukyanov wrote, “even if he were personally inclined to do so,” because a complete Ukrainian defeat would not win him any plaudits in the American political establishment.

Image

![Image 5: An air defense missile launcher, mounted on a wheeled trailer and sitting on snowy ground. Two armed people stand behind it, with a city in the distance.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/multimedia/13int-russia-putin-05-htqf/13int-russia-putin-05-htqf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A Patriot air defense system in Warsaw in 2023. Mr. Trump brokered a deal for Ukraine to acquire American weapons by allowing Europe to buy and sell the goods as a middle man.Credit...Kacper Pempel/Reuters
